title: Shaheen and DiLorenzo share thoughts on political issues as they fight for a spot in Congress - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM- On Oct. 5, the University of New Hampshire (UNH) hosted the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum in the Memorial Union Building. Republican nominee Anthony DiLorenzo and Democratic nominee Stefany Shaheen were both given 35 minutes to share their opinions on what issues in New Hampshire are important to them and what their goals are if they were to win the election on November third. Stefany Shaheen at the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum The conversation was hosted by the Carsey School of Public Policy. The Forum is a nonpartisan series for congressional nominees in New Hampshire. The conversation was moderated by Kevin Sullivan, UNH Alum and a Washington Post Pulitzer Prize Winner. One of Shaheen's main topics was ending the war in Iran: “We're now seeing $4 gas prices; this wasn't a reality till this war started.” Shaheen says that she has heard from at least one person every day in the last two weeks worrying about gas prices this winter. Shaheen wants to see this war come to an end, and points out the soldiers that have been lost through its duration. “We've got to bring an end to this war, and Congress can do it,” Shaheen says. DiLorenzo comments on the fact that “we can not be the world's police officers.”  He says he is not “for boots on the ground” in this war and doesn't support the fact that the Iranian government should have nuclear weapons. DiLorenzo finds it strange that an oil-producing country would need to produce nuclear energy, but he says that foreign policy is not at the top of his priority list. Anthony DiLorenzo at the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum When the topic of artificial intelligence was brought up, Shaheen expressed concerns. “We should be focused on innovation that lifts everyone up, not wipes everyone out,” Shaheen says. She urges Washington to put up guardrails. DiLorenzo points out that there is good and bad in all technology. While it can be scary and unknown, he trusts the experts when they say it's containable. He does agree with his opponent that there needs to be guardrails added “to ensure privacy is protected.” Throughout the debate, Shaheen comments on DiLorenzo's support of President Donald Trump. Trump has endorsed DiLorenzo for the Congressional District race. On social media, Trump calls DiLorenzo a “very successful Businessman and Entrepreneur,” which is a point DiLorenzo uses during his campaign. “We need more business people in D.C.,” DiLorenzo says. He points out that he has worked since he was 8 years old and calls his opponent privileged due to their family. Shaheen then comments on how ICE has affected the state of New Hampshire. “This is not helping our community be safer,” Shaheen says. She mentions that the Department of Homeland Security shared that only 5% of people who are being detained have been charged with violent crimes. Shaheen speaks on hearing personal stories from families affected by ICE. DiLorenzo comments that we need immigration reform and that policies should reflect what the country needs. He believes that there is room for improvement; law enforcement needs more training and proper training. Both candidates agree that there is a housing issue in the Granite State. DiLorenzo comments on the high cost of infrastructure, but is still in favor of building. He comments on the fact that housing prices are outpacing wages. Shaheen makes a point of the tariffs' effect on our country. “Tariffs have wreaked havoc,” Shaheen says. She makes a statement claiming DiLorenzo’s support of these tariffs. She believes that they are hurting small businesses. Each candidate was given a minute to close. Shaheen declares that she is going to work hard for change in this country, and for its people’s support. “We have a choice between change or more of the same,” Shaheen says. She again highlights her opponent's support for the tariffs, war, and Trump. Shaheen speaks directly to UNH students, telling them to vote. “Don't let anyone tell you you're not allowed to vote.” DiLorenzo considers the election to be a “simple choice.” He calls Shaheen a “political insider who has come from a fairly privileged family,” and points out that the experience he brings is hard work and business. “We need more common sense business leadership in D.C. and less professional politicians, and that's why I'm running,” DiLorenzo says. With the election coming up, many are wondering what's next and who will win at the polls.

title: Shannon Garvey: A UNH success story - The New Hampshire
content: In May of 2026, UNH English MFA (Master of Fine Arts) graduate Shannon Garvey received her first major publication with her novel, June Baby. Published and distributed by Random House and Thousand Voices Books, June Baby was a USA Today National Bestseller upon release, garnering acclaim from readers and critics alike. Bestselling author Coco Mellers describes the story as a “work of growing up” that is both “tender and precise,” with “Garvey’s prose [revealing] a writer of real emotional intelligence and depth.” The New York Times Book Review called the story an “old-fashioned love letter to summer romance, sun-fueled creativity and long rides on rusty bikes” — an “outsider’s story [that] unfolds in the voice of an insider.” Throughout our conversation, Garvey touched on what it has felt like to be propelled into literary success. In regards to the book tour she embarked on over the summer, she emphasized how “amazing [it was] to see [June Baby] connect with readers.” She goes on to say, “I spent four years writing it...I’m sure I would be nervous if I was talking about anything else in the world, but this is the one thing that I know best.” June Baby opens with seventeen year-old Ruth who, after losing her mother to cancer, leaves to live on a wealthy remote island with renowned photographer Diana Beckett. Ten years later, after tragedy upends her life again, Ruth must embark on a journey of mystery and self-discovery to reexamine everything she thought she knew about her past. It’s a coming-of-age story that explores both love and grief, embracing the duality between loss and possibility in one’s life. Describing her process, Garvey says that “writing a novel is such an experience, in empathy and curiosity; every day, curious to see where the story is going to lead and exercising this really beautiful empathy for characters that might not exist, but you are, every second, wondering how it might feel to be them in this scenario.” Garvey then discusses her emotional and physical attachment to a specific place, and how that manifested through her characters. “With Ruth, I was really interested in writing about somebody who was in love with a place, so the book is set on Block Island, a very small island off of Rhode Island,” the state in which Garvey herself grew up. She states she has been “fascinated by Block Island since [she] was a child,” and, through her writing, has been enamoured with the question of “what somebody might do to hold onto a place that they love that much.” Garvey makes it clear that Ruth is not her, but some of Ruth’s “fears and thoughts about the world” are things Garvey has thought and felt at various points in her life. “These characters aren't people you know at all, but to write them, you are drawing on that reservoir of your own emotions and your own connections to others.” As impressive as her novel’s acclaim is for an author and their debut work, Garvey is not the only one ecstatic about her recent success. In fact, she began writing June Baby while studying in UNH’s English MFA program, where the book eventually flourished into her thesis. She details the process. “The MFA thesis has to be 150 pages, and it can either be a collection of short stories or a novel excerpt,” but the workshop-based program “is really built around short stories...I knew from the beginning that I wanted my thesis to be a novel because I wanted to have the opportunity to have incredible writers like Tom [Payne] and Ann Williams and Jaed Coffin have their eyes on it…I thought that would be really valuable.” Of her time in the MFA program, she says “that there’s something really special about being one around a group of people who are taking the same thing you are very seriously…there’s something really transformational about inhaling that much work.” According to writer, professor, and head of the MFA department Thomas Payne, “the MFA program in Creative Writing has graduated any number of stellar writers of poetry, fiction and memoir over our last 50 years as a nationally-known program. But for Shannon to rocket out of UNH onto the Today show with basically her MFA thesis (this novel) a couple of years after graduating? That's just jaw dropping.” Garvey graduated in 2017 with a B.A. in Neuroscience and Behavior, and while in the MFA program, she taught undergraduate classes. These formative years provided her with an ever-deepening understanding of writing, literature, and what it means to find yourself through a work of art. Payne describes the “feeling” he had that Garvey was “going to hit a home run” after years of “knowing her fiction [and] seeing drafts of [June Baby].” In addition to June Baby’s popularity, Garvey has made a name for herself through her shorter works in the Saturday Evening Post and her feature on the Peabody-Award winning Moth Radio Hour. Now, after being on the “Today” show—which she considers to have been “incredibly surreal”—and in a variety of national magazines from Vogue to People, Garvey is well-underway on her second novel. “My way of dealing with the unknowns of this industry is always to be grateful for what has come to pass, and do the work every day…then, you know, we’ll see what happens.” Catch Shannon Garvey’s reading and Q&A for UNH’s Writer Series on Thursday, Oct. 22 at 5pm in Hamilton Smith Hall. The event was organized by Thomas Payne and the MFA department, and he hopes that “any UNH undergrad who wants to be a writer” comes to the event.

title: UNH falls to Monmouth on family weekend - The New Hampshire
content: The Monmouth Hawks traveled to take on the New Hampshire Wildcats on Oct. 17th. The Hawks weren't the only ones who traveled on Saturday. UNH also hosted its annual Family Weekend. UNH has held its Family Weekend for the past 15 years, typically in mid-October, as seen this year. Families participated in campus tours, daily life, arts performances, community gatherings, and a slew of athletic games, aimed at promoting community, connection, and the celebration of new students and a new academic year. The stands were packed with proud UNH families who were ready to watch their kids win over the Hawks. However, the game took a quick turn as the Hawks went up 21-0 by the end of the first quarter. The Wildcats’ defense really showed up in the second with almost a scoreless quarter, but the brutal Hawks offense scored again with just 21 seconds remaining in the half. UNH opened the second half with a touchdown, and Monmouth retaliated with another. With UNH finally in the game, the third quarter concluded. Unfortunately for Monmouth, they started the final 15 minutes with a turnover that led to a UNH touchdown. The Hawks also scored 7, but UNH followed with another TD. Although the UNH offense killed it in the final minutes of the game, their effort wasn't enough as the final score was 42-21. As the UNH students said goodbye to their families and the Monmouth players, they hoped to greet a victory next week as the Wildcats travel to face Merrimack.

title: The Learning Landscape: The New England Agroforester - Fall Equinox 2026 - University of New Hampshire
content: ADAPT’s second Agroforestry Educator Cohort launched this July with a two-day immersive learning experience, gathering 13 educators from Vermont, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts. Beginning at Dartmouth College, Professor Theresa Ong and graduate student Krystal Bagnaschi introduced participants to key agroforestry concepts and shared the goals and vision of the ADAPT program. The group then toured several research and demonstration sites, including two food forests, the Experimental Linear Gap (ELG) research area, where a variety of forest farming crops are being studied, and an edible riparian buffer designed to support both ecological and food production goals. The riparian buffer was established in partnership with ReTreeUS, and Executive Director Richard Hodges joined the group to discuss food forest design and the organization's growing network of high school food forests throughout New England. On the second day, participants visited the Abenaki Garden in Hartford, Vermont, where Earl Hatley shared the story of the Community and Culture Acre, a teaching garden that also produces food and seeds for local food banks. Alongside the traditional Three Sisters planting, the site features hazelnuts, elderberries, ground cherries, and blueberries, with ongoing efforts to expand the area into a mature food forest system. The cohort concluded its field experience at Howling Wolf Farm in Randolph, Vermont, where Jenn Colby showcased her innovative approach to creating silvopasture through ecological succession. Participants learned how rotationally grazed sheep are integrated into the landscape, helping transform emerging woodlands into productive agroforestry systems while supporting animal welfare and ecosystem health. Looking ahead, both Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 participants will continue their field-based learning in Year 2 of the program. Upcoming visits include The Ecology School in Saco, Maine, on October 5 and the New Hampshire State Forest Nursery in Boscawen, NH, on November 13. For more information, contact State Coordinator Mike Smith at 4-H Community Agriculture and NH Ag in the Classroom. Two educators from the UNH Extension agroforestry program were recently featured on the Northeast Farm to School Collaborative's podcast, The Farm to School Podcast. Becky Denslow, a participant in the second Maple Tales cohort and now a member of the second ADAPT Agroforestry cohort, joined Mary Hartigan Demers, a member of the first ADAPT Agroforestry cohort, to share their experiences bringing agroforestry and maple education into their schools. The conversation highlights how educators are creating meaningful connections between students, trees, food systems, and local landscapes. Mary discusses developing a maple sugaring program at her middle school in downtown Manchester, and Becky reflects on her continuing agroforestry journey through multiple UNH Extension programs. An upcoming episode will feature Megan Glenn and other program leaders discussing the ADAPT Agroforestry program and cohorts, helping share lessons and successes from educators across the region. Listen to the episode on the Northeast Farm to School Collaborative's podcast page: The Farm to School Podcast. Members of the ADAPT Team participated in Erik Schellenberg's Temperate Syntropic Agroforestry webinar in August 2026. Drawing on his experience developing syntropic agroforestry systems in southern New York, Erik shared practical lessons, observations, and reflections from the field. Resources from the presentation include: Building on the introductory session, a second webinar on December 3, 2026 will take a deeper look at the theory, principles, and ecological relationships that underpin syntropic agroforestry. While some foundational concepts will be revisited, the session will be valuable for both those returning and those new to the approach. Participants are encouraged to bring questions about adapting syntropic practices to temperate climates. For more information, contact Jonathan Bates at Cornell Cooperative Extension. ReTreeUS Founder and Program Manager Richard Hodges prepares to plant a tree at a school site. Image credit: ReTreeUS. Discussions at the recent ADAPT all-hands meeting emphasized a challenge familiar to many agroforestry practitioners: how to establish educational plantings that remain productive, relevant, and well-maintained over time. ReTreeUS, a nonprofit organization working throughout New England, has spent the past 15 years developing and refining systems designed specifically to address those challenges in school settings. Founded by Richard Hodges, ReTreeUS began with a focus on helping schools create outdoor learning spaces centered around orchards and gardens. Over time, the organization found that long-term success depended not only on planting trees and gardens but also on developing practical approaches to maintenance, educator engagement, and curriculum integration. To date, ReTreeUS has helped establish more than 120 school and community orchards across Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and Massachusetts. The organization originally set a goal of creating 100 school community orchards and has since expanded its focus to include school food forests. Over the next three years, the organization plans to establish 30 school food forests, including seven new sites this year. Foresters, farmers, technical advisors, service partners, and researchers observing tree plantings at a forest farming site at the ADAPT Project’s Fall 2026 All-Hands meeting. The ReTreeUS approach centers around systems that fit the realities of school operations. School gardens often face challenges related to summer maintenance, staff turnover, and weed management. To address these, ReTreeUS developed a "back-to-school garden" model. Schools receive trays of established crops such as lettuce and kale sourced from nearby farms. Students plant the seedlings in September, allowing gardens to become immediately productive while reducing summer maintenance demands. Cover crops help suppress weeds, improve soil health, and support pollinators during periods when students are not present. The organization's orchard model similarly prioritizes long-term stewardship. Typical school orchard plantings include 12 to 20 semi-dwarf fruit trees, often apples, pears, and peaches. ReTreeUS has developed deer-management strategies, planting protocols, and maintenance resources that schools can implement after installation. Teacher caretakers may receive stipends for ongoing stewardship, accompanied by progress reports and photographs documenting orchard development. Educational resources are another core component of the model. ReTreeUS provides standards-aligned lessons, presentations, videos, and enrichment materials that help teachers use orchards and food forests as living classrooms. By connecting outdoor spaces directly to existing curricula, orchards become more fully integrated into school operations and student learning. The organization's current food forest initiative expands on lessons learned through its orchard program. While each site is adapted to local conditions, plantings typically include multiple layers of perennial food-producing species. Fruit and nut trees may be combined with blueberries, raspberries, strawberries, grapevines, hazelnuts, perennial herbs, native plums, bush cherries, Cornelian cherries, and nitrogen-fixing species such as gomi. Clover is commonly seeded throughout the site as a living groundcover that suppresses weeds and contributes nitrogen to the system. One challenge ReTreeUS has worked to address is the perception that food forests are difficult to manage or appear untidy. School sites often require landscapes that are both ecologically functional and visually organized. Sheet mulching, straw, paper, defined planting zones, and groundcover establishment reduce competition from weeds while maintaining an appearance appropriate for educational campuses. Many of these plantings begin producing harvestable crops within the first year, particularly berries, herbs, and other perennial species. This early productivity helps sustain student interest while providing opportunities to explore topics such as food production, ecology, pollination, soil health, and agroforestry. Feedback from participating schools consistently highlights student engagement. Educators report that outdoor learning environments often create opportunities for students who may struggle in traditional classroom settings to participate in different ways. Planting, observing, harvesting, and caring for perennial systems allows students to engage directly with ecological processes over multiple seasons. For ADAPT partners exploring agroforestry in educational settings, the ReTreeUS model offers a practical example of how long-term stewardship, curriculum integration, and maintenance planning can support the success of school-based agroforestry projects. As interest in school food forests continues to grow across New England, these experiences provide useful insights into how agroforestry systems can become lasting educational and community assets. Civil Eats' Summer 2026 Food and Farming Book Guide hits several relevant themes for agroforestry in the Northeast: perennial agriculture, Indigenous ecological knowledge, soil health, environmental contamination, and community-led food systems. While the guide covers a wide range of topics, a handful of titles stand out for agroforestry practitioners, educators, and technical service providers. For New England agroforesters, these titles offer both practical insights and a broader perspective on the forces shaping the future of regenerative agriculture, conservation, and tree-based farming systems. Investors often turn to recommendations made by Wall Street analysts before making a Buy, Sell, or Hold decision about a stock. While media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm employed (or sell-side) analysts often affect a stock's price, do they really matter? Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about UnitedHealth Group (UNH) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage. UnitedHealth currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.54, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 27 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.54 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy. Of the 27 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 18 are Strong Buy and three are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 66.7% and 11.1% of all recommendations. Check price target & stock forecast for UnitedHealth here>>> The ABR suggests buying UnitedHealth, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation. Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations. This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements. Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision. Although both Zacks Rank and ABR are displayed in a range of 1--5, they are different measures altogether. Broker recommendations are the sole basis for calculating the ABR, which is typically displayed in decimals (such as 1.28). The Zacks Rank, on the other hand, is a quantitative model designed to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5. It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. Because of their employers' vested interests, these analysts issue more favorable ratings than their research would support, misguiding investors far more often than helping them. On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements. Furthermore, the different grades of the Zacks Rank are applied proportionately across all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide earnings estimates for the current year. In other words, at all times, this tool maintains a balance among the five ranks it assigns. Another key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank is freshness. The ABR is not necessarily up-to-date when you look at it. But, since brokerage analysts keep revising their earnings estimates to account for a company's changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in indicating future price movements. title: SHARPP hosts annual 'Take Back the Night' event - The New Hampshire
content: On the night of Thursday Oct. 15, on the Thompson Hall lawn at the University of New Hampshire, the SHARPP Center for Interpersonal Violence Awareness, Prevention, and Advocacy hosted its annual Take Back the Night (TBTN) event, an event that has been hosted since 1981. TBTN is an awareness event for victims of interpersonal violence. The event calls people to action and holds a vigil. While some attendees were wrapping chilled hands around warm cups of apple cider, tea, or hot chocolate provided by UNH catering, others were busy creating posters with encouraging messages reminding people they are never alone. “This event is important, it’s showing campus how interpersonal violence affects campus, and it gives survivors a place to speak and be heard where they otherwise aren't able to be,” said Rachel Stewart, the director of SHARPP. As the event opened, every attendee was given a glowstick which was later used in an activity to show how every person at the event had been impacted by interpersonal violence, either directly or indirectly. UNH Acapella group, The New Hampshire Notables have performed at the past three TBTN events. This year they chose to perform the song “Can't Catch Me Now” by Olivia Rodrigo, to highlight the struggle and resilience of interpersonal violence survivors. Their contribution was a moment of calm to help attendees transition into the open mic segment of the event. At the start of the open mic, Stewart briefly mentioned recent events at Cornell University involving interpersonal violence, highlighting its ubiquitous nature on college campuses. The event then moved into the speaker portion of the open mic. “I want people to know that this community is for them,” said Darian Kavlahao, one of the event MCs for TBTN. Many attendees got the opportunity to either speak or listen to the stories of others, sharing awareness and creating a supportive and inclusive environment. “[Interpersonal violence] is a part of my story, but it is not the whole story.” said Emma Schmidl-Gagne, a community advisor for SHARPP and the other event MC. While many were sharing their stories, each attendee was also given a candle that was lit and held for the remainder of the event. As the event ended with many feeling less alone, Stewart reminds all that this does not end here. “This event is great, but it can't just be one night. Everyone needs to care about interpersonal violence, it has to be every day,” Stewart said. SHARPP Center resources are available for all. The SHARPP Center is located on the 3rd Floor of Smith Hall. Resources include scheduling a meeting or contacting the SHARPP office at (603) 862- 3494. SHARPP also has a 24/7 helpline at (603) 862-7233. Drop-in hours have been temporarily paused for Fall 2026 due to staffing constraints. However, you can still stop by or contact SHARPP to make a virtual or in-person appointment. The SHARPP Center offers confidential appointments and a safe space to meet with staff and representatives.

title: UnitedHealth Beats Q3 2026 Earnings and Raises Outlook - TradingView
content: · UnitedHealth beat Q3 forecasts and raised 2026 profit guidance. · Lower medical costs boosted margins despite falling membership. · Rising costs and regulatory risks remain key challenges for 2027. UnitedHealth Group beat Wall Street third-quarter 2026 forecasts on the 13th of October and raised its full-year profit outlook for the third time this year.1 Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $4.69 against a $4.12 consensus, and 2026 guidance now stands at no less than $20.50.1 Here's what drove the beat, what changed, and what it could mean for UNH investors. · Earnings beat: adjusted EPS of $4.69 vs $4.12 expected; revenue of $112.7 billion vs $111.0 billion.1 · Margin recovery: the medical care ratio fell to 88.4% from 89.9%, helped by $610 million of reserve releases.1 · Guidance raised: 2026 adjusted EPS of at least $20.50, up from $19.50–$20.00.1 · Weak spot: members fell to 48.3 million from 50.1 million a year earlier. · Stock reaction: shares have risen more than 7% after brokers lifted targets. This was a margin-recovery quarter, not a growth quarter. Revenue actually slipped 0.4% year on year as UnitedHealthcare shed members on purpose. But earnings from operations jumped 52% to $6.6 billion, and the repair job that began after the 2025 collapse is now visible in every segment.1 UnitedHealth Q3 2026 Earnings Are Up 61% Amid Easing Medical Costs Adjusted EPS rose 61% to $4.69 from $2.92, while GAAP EPS climbed to $4.56 from $2.59. Net margin nearly doubled to 3.6% from 2.1%.1 Net earnings attributable to shareholders reached $4.1 billion, up from $2.3 billion a year earlier.2 The important medical care ratio (MCR) is at 88.4%, below analyst forecasts.3 Management credited cost management, benefit cuts and pricing discipline. However, the quarter included $610 million of favourable prior-period reserve development for 2026 dates of service, which flattered the ratio.1 The operating cost ratio also improved to 12.8% from 13.5%.1 Optum Health is the standout turnaround. Revenue fell 10% as the unit exited value-based care markets where it lacked scale, yet operating earnings rose almost eighteen-fold to $735 million.1 Optum Rx benefited from biosimilar adoption, although adjusted scripts dropped to 393 million from 414 million.1 The soft spot was membership. UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people, below the 48.6 million analysts expected and down from 50.1 million a year ago.2 Medicare Advantage enrolment has contracted by 935,000 since year-end 2025. Cash flow from operations was $5.1 billion, or 1.2x net income.1 Why the Medical Care Ratio is Important for UNH Stock The medical care ratio (MCR) shows how much of each premium dollar UnitedHealth spends on patient care. At 88.4%, about 88 cents of every dollar went on medical costs, leaving the rest for running costs and profit. Small moves matter at this scale. On roughly $87 billion of quarterly premiums, a one-point drop in the MCR frees up close to $0.9 billion of profit before tax.1 That is why investors watch this one number more closely than revenue. The strongest signal from the report was the improved full-year outlook. UnitedHealth raised its forecast for 2026 adjusted earnings to at least $20.50 per share, up from its previous range of $19.50 to $20.00. The revised target also exceeded the analyst consensus of approximately $19.86 before the announcement.1 The raise is cautious in shape. Nine-month adjusted EPS already stands at $18.30, so the floor implies only about $2.20 for the fourth quarter. That leaves room for typical Q4 seasonality in Optum Health, plus extra technology spending, which management flagged on the call. It also leaves room for another upside surprise in January. Capital returns remain intact. The company bought back $5.0 billion of stock and paid $6.2 billion of dividends through September. Debt-to-capital was 41.7%, against a target of about 40% by year-end.1 Commercial medical costs remain the main pressure point. UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said commercial cost trend is running above the company's initial 11% assumption, driven by specialty drugs, higher clinician costs and No Surprises Act arbitration. He conceded this pushes out the timeline for long-term commercial margin targets and stressed that the trend is stabilising, not accelerating. Employer attrition also cost 165,000 members in the quarter.1 Medicare Advantage: smaller, but more profitable. The deliberate shrink-to-profit strategy continues, with 935,000 fewer MA seniors since year-end 2025.1 According to executives Medicare margins should end 2026 near the top of the 2-4% target range. Medicaid is still a drag. Core Medicaid margins should improve only to modestly better than −1% for 2026, with a return to target margins aimed for 2028. Optum Health's repair is ahead of schedule. Leaving sub-scale value-based care markets lifted the margin to 3.2%, against a 6-8% target for 2028. Optum Insight's AI-driven Integrity One platform has grown from two live clients at the end of 2025 to 15, with 24 more in progress. Reputation and regulatory reset. Management is cutting 30% of prior-approval volume by end-2026, has launched a fee-based, transparent PBM model and plans 100% rebate pass-through by January 2028.1 It is also rebating 2026 ACA individual-market profits to about 1 million members. The Justice Department legal actions over UnitedHealth's Medicare business remain an unresolved overhang. The Street's verdict is constructive: most large brokers kept buy-equivalent ratings and several raised targets after the print. CFO DeVeydt said the low end of the 13–16% long-term EPS growth target is a reasonable starting point for 2027 and hinted that consensus may understate the opportunity. Applied to the $20.50 floor, 13% growth implies roughly $23.15 of 2027 adjusted EPS, above the $22.61 consensus. A fuller 2027 outlook is due before year-end. The bull case rests on margin repair. Morgan Stanley argues that the UnitedHealthcare-Optum combination is hard to copy and that cost normalisation should pull margins back toward historical levels.4 Goldman Sachs, per a published summary of its note, sees further profit leverage in Optum Health, commercial and Medicaid.5 Piper Sandler values the shares at 18x estimated 2028 EPS.6 At about 17x forward earnings, the stock trades below its own history. The bear case is about growth and quality. Membership keeps shrinking, and the stock is down roughly 10% over three months even as rivals held steady. The Q3 MCR beat leaned on $610 million of reserve releases, which will not repeat on schedule. Commercial cost trend, Medicaid funding, Star ratings and the DOJ investigation are the swing factors for 2027. UnitedHealth has now beaten and raised three times in 2026, and the profit recovery looks durable. The next catalyst is the full 2027 outlook due before year-end, where investors will want proof that earnings can grow even while enrolment does not. content: Quick Answer: As of Tuesday, October 20, UnitedHealth Group (UNH) was trading at approximately $421.50, up around 3.5% on the day and extending a rebound from the $362.74 October low. The rebound is a continuation of a move stemming from the company’s Q3 results, which it said reflect “the discipline and execution” of its teams. The company also raised its full-year guidance for the third time this year, taking the 2026 adjusted EPS floor to $20.50. On the daily chart, the stock has broken a descending trendline from the July highs and is currently pressing the 61.8% Fibonacci level at $421.87. My view: UNH is bullish as long as it trades above $399.37. A break above $421.87 would likely lead to a target of $440.19 and $458.51. UNH was up around 3.51% on Tuesday, more than double the 1.54% move in the healthcare services and equipment sector. No news was reported to have caused the move. This puts Tuesday’s rally as an extension of the move the stock started on Wednesday, October 14, the day after the company reported Q3 results. For the quarter, UnitedHealth Group reported an adjusted EPS of $4.69, topping the $4.14 consensus, and the company cited “disciplined execution”. As a result, the company raised its full-year guidance to a minimum of $20.50, from its prior range of $19.50 to $20.00. Revenue during the quarter fell to $112.7 billion from $113.2 billion in the same quarter last year. However, earnings from operations improved to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion, the medical care ratio improved to 88.4% from 89.9% and UnitedHealthcare’s operating margin improved to 3.3% from 2.1%. The company has purposely shed members. At the end of the quarter, UnitedHealthcare had 48.3 million members, down from 50.1 million a year earlier, and the company lost 935,000 members in its Medicare Advantage plans since year-end 2025. I would say the quality of the margin is the more interesting question. The current quarter had $610 million of favorable prior-period reserve development. Management also said commercial cost trends are running above its initial 11% assumption, and its 2027 pricing is based on the assumption those costs would continue. In the quarter, Optum Health lost 10% of its revenue to $22.9 billion, largely due to the loss of value-based care patients. But it was still able to improve its operating earnings to $735 million, compared to $41 million last year. Optum’s other units also improved. OptumInsight improved earnings to $1.3 billion from $920 million and Optum Rx improved earnings to $1.7 billion from $1.5 billion. Optum Rx now has more than 50 percent of its membership from external clients, further reducing its reliance on UnitedHealthcare members. Operating cash flow of $5.1 billion, or 1.2 times net income, funded share repurchases and the $9.28 annual dividend. According to CFO Wayne DeVeydt on the latest earnings call, analyst consensus for 2027 “may understate the opportunity ahead.” DeVeydt added that a starting point for 2027 might be the low end of the company’s 13% to 16% long-term growth target, which is 13%. With 13% growth on the current $20.50 floor, we would see EPS at $23.17 in 2027, per calculations by Stocktwits. Management has said they will provide a more robust 2027 outlook by year-end. Risks for 2027 are mainly with the company’s Medicare Advantage (MA) business. About 69% of members in 2027 are in 4-Star or greater plans; a reduction from the current year. Plus, about 390,000 members are in MA plans that will not be offered in 2027. Also, two Medicare Advantage investigations by the DOJ remain open. UNH’s stock price, about $421.50, puts it at 20.6 times the 2026 EPS floor and 18.2 times the implied 2027 EPS. Post-earnings targets cluster around these numbers. Baird cut its target to $427, Barclays to $440, and Raymond James to $450, per Benzinga. More bullish targets include $504 from Piper Sandler and $500 from Bernstein, which cut from $512. The stock trades just under the lower targets, and with the latest Q3 beat, and an anticipated 2027 outlook by year-end, I think the upside is greater than the 2027 outlook. UnitedHealth is currently trading at $421.50, a 3.5% gain on the day, and is extending a sharp rebound after dropping to $362.74 in October, which was close to the 200 day EMA. The stock has not only cleared the 50 day EMA at $388.37, but also a descending trend line from the July peak, making the near term trend bullish. One thing worth noting is that price has reached the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level at $421.87, which is often a make-or-break level and in this case could indicate where the recent recovery stops. The 14 day relative strength index (RSI) has hit an overbought level at 72.10, the first time this has happened since May. Similar to the above reasoning, I view this as a caution flag. Above current resistance at $421.87, the next resistance levels are $440.19, which is the Barclays price target, and then the July high at $458.51. The current level of support at $410.51 is also the 50% Fibonacci retracement level. Below that is support at $399.37, which is the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement level, and below that the key level at $388.37 to $385.23, which is where the 50 day EMA meets the 23.6% Fibonacci retracement, and below that is the 200 day EMA and the October low at $362.74. I am bullish as long as UnitedHealth remains above $399.37. A break below that level would put focus on $388.37 and $385.23 and a close below the 50 day EMA would also be bearish. UnitedHealth Group (UNH) extended its post-earnings rally on Tuesday after reporting Q3 results and raising its 2026 guidance for the third time. UNH stock gained about 3.5% on the day, more than double the gain of the healthcare services sector. The key level is the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level at $421.87. A daily close above that level opens up $440.19 and the July high at $458.51. Management has stated they would issue a fuller 2027 outlook by year-end. They have not specified a date, but results for Q4 are expected to be released in late January 2027.

title: Honorary Degree Surprise for 101st Birthday Brings Wildcats From Two Generations Together - University of New Hampshire
content: Dan Carr ’85 and Dr. Julian Silverblatt at Silverblatt's 101st birthday celebration. When you have as much time for comparison under your belt as Dr. Julian Silverblatt does, certain proclamations can carry a little more weight. Silverblatt recently declared his 101st birthday – celebrated this summer in his hometown of Houston, Texas – his best one yet. Given the catalog of calendar flips he had to choose from, such a stance felt particularly momentous. Then again, given the circumstances, it also didn’t seem all that far-fetched. It’s not every day that you turn 101 years old in a room full of friends and family wearing a borrowed cap and gown while receiving an honorary degree from a beloved institution, a degree presented by someone who went from perfect stranger to future family Christmas card recipient in a matter of hours. Silverblatt was surprised on his 101st birthday with an honorary degree from UNH, a special delivery cooked up by his daughters to honor their father’s cherished time as a student while he was in the military. Circumstances of his arrangement ultimately prevented him from graduating, but he always looked back on his Durham days fondly. The family wanted the degree presented by someone with UNH connections, and that person wound up being Dan Carr ’85, a fellow Houston resident who had never even heard of the Silverblatt family when Julian’s daughters cold-called him at work one afternoon to make a pitch for his assistance. Carr was happy to oblige, the honorary degree was presented, and by the end of the celebration, Silverblatt was the proud owner of both a treasured UNH memento and a meaningful friendship forged with a fellow Wildcat more than 40 years his junior. “He said, ‘This is the best birthday I’ve ever had.’ It really meant a lot to him,” Terri Brown, the oldest of Julian’s three daughters, says. “He was totally surprised. Someone asked me if he cried, and he’s not a crier, but the smile on his face said it all.” It was a whirlwind experience for all involved. The family had to pass on UNH’s invitation for Silverblatt to attend commencement to receive the degree – even though her father “walks faster than me, still drives and takes himself to get his haircut whenever he needs to,” Terri quips. In the end Silverblatt’s daughters – Terri and sisters Pamela and Cindy – wound up with less than a week to find a UNH representative who could be on hand for the celebration in Houston. And Carr, for his part, was working in his office on an otherwise normal Wednesday when he received a phone call from the office receptionist. “I got a call from reception and she said, ‘I’ve got three daughters on the line that want to talk to you.’ It was Cindy who spoke, and she said, ‘Are you Dan Carr? Are you a grad of UNH? Because I’ve got a really strange request to ask of you,’” Carr says. So how did the family come to choose Carr as the potential UNH representative? A quick Google search and an alphabetical list. It was Cindy who did the sleuthing, finding a guest list from a UNH alumni reception held at the Houston Space Center in 2020 (only days before the start of the COVID shutdown). She decided to start alphabetically at the top of the list and begin making cold calls. It only took one. Though Carr, the first name on the list, had never met a member of the family prior to the phone call, his involvement was a pretty easy sell. Beyond the endearingly quirky nature of the story, the situation prompted him to think of his own father, who at 96 years old had just entered home hospice care. “I’m really happy they reached out to me, because my dad had not been doing so well, so it feels really good to be able to help out another family who wanted to come together for their father,” says Carr. For the celebration, Terri and her sisters secured a cap and gown from Silverblatt’s daughter-in-law, Shelley Silverblatt, asked their father to don it, and had Carr surprise him with the honorary degree. But that was only the beginning of the connection. The pair spent the rest of the brunch becoming fast friends. “What’s really cool is that the thing we had in common is that we walked the same campus about 40 years apart,” Carr says. “It was really neat to share stories with him and his family about that, to learn about his experience at UNH and beyond. His daughters said, ‘Dan, please give us your address because we want to make sure you are part of our Christmas card circulation.’” “He could have been a long-lost member of the family. It was just incredible to pick a stranger out of the clear blue sky and have him be so personable and just fit so seamlessly with our family,” says Terri. “That to me was overwhelming, just how wonderful Dan was. I can’t sing his praises enough. He just made the day that much more special.” Silverblatt’s UNH story is a unique one very much of his time. Originally from Cincinnati, Ohio, Silverblatt was assigned to UNH through the Army Specialized Training Program (ASTP) during World War II. The program, created in 1942, identified academically talented enlisted men and sent them to college campuses for accelerated training in engineering, foreign languages, medicine, and other specialized technical fields. Silverblatt completed pre-medical coursework at UNH from 1943 to 1944. Although he didn’t graduate, his academic work at UNH was a key piece in enabling him to enroll in medical school without first earning an undergraduate degree. Silverblatt went on to earn his medical degree from the University of Cincinnati and served for more than 50 years as a practicing physician in the Houston area. “He was taking almost exclusively science classes” at UNH, Terri says, and before he left, he had “completed all the science requirements for going to medical school, so the Army just sent him on to medical school at the University of Cincinnati. He was 19 years old when he started there and didn’t have a bachelor’s degree.” Carr arrived on UNH’s campus about four decades later, and met his wife, Kari Kaalstad, while they were both students (the couple celebrated their 37th wedding anniversary in June). He looks back fondly on his days as a student and member of the rowing team at UNH and also participated for three years in helping to lead orientation for first-year students. “I have some friends for life from those years, that’s for sure,” Carr says. He may have made another in Silverblatt. The two talked about a lot more than just their individual times as UNH students, connecting over each other’s family histories and baseball rooting interests (Carr’s father grew up rooting for the New York/San Francisco Giants, and Silverblatt supported the Cincinnati Reds). They also talked hobbies, and although some of those overlap a little less, a future reconnection could still be in the cards. “It was just really fun to connect with him. I’d love to see him again – even though I don’t play bridge,” Carr quips. “It was really fun, and it’s amazing that it was UNH that brought us together.” Given all of the logistics involved, the celebration couldn’t have come together any better. Silverblatt’s daughters were able to honor their father and commemorate an important time in his life while also creating an unexpected connection across UNH generations. Silverblatt and Carr had distinctly different experiences at UNH, but both have reason to draw on lasting memories as students that impacted them for decades beyond their time on campus. And the birthday celebration put them in the same room to do so together. Which begs the question, what exactly does Silverblatt’s family have planned for an encore? “I am all about doing whatever I can to make him happy, and it’s funny because people have asked me, ‘what are you going to do next year?’ I honestly don’t know, but it’s going to take me a little while to think of something that could top this one,” Terri says. title: Visiting UNH? Five reasons to also tour UNH's College of Life Sciences and Agriculture - University of New Hampshire
content: If you're interested in life sciences, agriculture, environmental science, nutrition, genetics, marine biology, or any of the programs in UNH’s College of Life Sciences and Agriculture, a dedicated COLSA academic tour gives you a closer look at the college, the people, and the opportunities that would shape your four years here. Here are five reasons it's worth adding a COLSA tour to your campus visit and admissions general tour.Register for a UNH COLSA academic tour 1. You'll see the spaces where COLSA students work, do research, and learn The UNH general admissions tour shows you residence halls, dining, and the main campus. A COLSA academic tour takes you into the college’s classrooms, teaching and research labs, and research facilities. COLSA students work across a range of hands-on environments like research labs, greenhouses, animal facilities, and field sites connected to New Hampshire's forests, farms, and coastline. Seeing some of those spaces in person helps you understand what "hands-on learning" looks like in your field of interest, before you commit. 2. You can ask questions that are specific to your COLSA major interests A COLSA academic tour is designed specifically for students interested in the college's programs and majors. Current COLSA students lead the tour, and faculty get involved, too. Every tour includes a Q&A session with a faculty member where you can ask questions about specific majors, research opportunities, and what life looks like as a COLSA student. If you're trying to decide between majors, like wildlife and conservation biology and environmental conservation and sustainability, or between the nutrition dietetics option and the health and wellness option, this is the right place to ask. 3. You'll get a clearer picture of where a degree from UNH’s College of Life Sciences and Agriculture can take you One of the most common questions prospective students and families have is: “What can I actually do with this degree?” COLSA's outcomes data offers a starting point. The most recent First Destination Survey shows 93% of COLSA grads are employed or in graduate school. During the tour, you’ll hear directly from current students and faculty about how those outcomes connect to specific programs, internships, and research experiences. Alumni have been in roles like Public Program Educator at the Audubon Society of Rhode Island and Community Outreach Manager for the Seacoast Science Center Marine Mammal Rescue Program. A COLSA visit gives you the chance to ask how students get from the classroom to careers like those. 4. A COLSA tour can help you figure out your major, even if you're undecided You don't need to have your major figured out before you visit. In fact, many UNH first-year students arrive on campus undeclared or change their major at least once before graduating. A COLSA academic session can help you start narrowing things down. That's a wide range of fields, so visiting COLSA, hearing how faculty and students describe the work, and seeing labs in person can help you identify which direction feels right, or rule out options that don't. If you're still exploring after you’re a Wildcat, COLSA's St. Martin Career Exploration Office is a resource for students working through those questions once they're enrolled. 5. Why visiting UNH’s College of Life Sciences and Agriculture before you apply is worth your time Visiting before you apply or before you commit is one of the most practical things you can do to make this important decision with more confidence. A COLSA academic tour is an opportunity to see the college as it is, ask more in depth questions, and get a feel for whether this is the right environment for you. If you're already planning to visit UNH, adding a COLSA academic session to your itinerary can give you significantly more information to work with when making your college decisions. title: Occupational Therapy Conference Returns to UNH for Third Year - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH will welcome occupational therapy professionals and students from across the state and region on Nov. 14 for the New Hampshire Occupational Therapy Association (NHOTA) Fall Conference. It marks the third consecutive year UNH has hosted the annual conference, which has grown significantly in recent years. Organizers expect between 150 and 200 attendees this fall, compared with roughly 30 to 40 participants when the conference was smaller. The conference brings together occupational therapists for a day of continuing education and professional collaboration, including a keynote presentation, breakout sessions and scholarly poster presentations. For UNH, it also provides an opportunity to bring professionals to campus while showcasing the work of occupational therapy students and faculty. "We love hosting the conference. In a way, it feels like welcoming guests into our home,” says Casey Rabideau, clinical assistant professor of occupational therapy and UNH's liaison to NHOTA. “It is an opportunity to bring visibility to our program, build alumni relationships, and showcase our work at many different levels." UNH students will have an active presence at the conference, presenting research from honors projects, master's theses, and doctoral capstones, while faculty will also lead conference sessions. This year's presentations highlight the range of work happening at UNH. Rabideau will join students and Sarah Valli from the UNH Institute on Disability for a session on improving access to assistive technology. Their work includes an initiative in which students use 3D printing to create assistive devices for people with disabilities across New Hampshire. Other presentations will explore socially assistive robots for Alzheimer's and dementia home care, artificial intelligence's potential role in occupational therapy, and how occupational therapy fieldwork and doctoral capstone students can support school systems. Beyond the presentations, Rabideau says the conference gives students a chance to network directly with professionals in the field. "Our state is small, so having close to 175 practitioners come together is quite significant," Rabideau says. "For our students, that one-on-one interaction is important. They might meet someone from a future fieldwork site or hear about a job opening. It creates opportunities to network and start thinking about career pathways." The conference will also feature a keynote panel from the Krempels Center, where individuals will share their lived experiences with disability and occupational therapy, helping practitioners reconnect with the impact and purpose of their work. Hosting the conference comes at a time of growth for UNH's occupational therapy program. The program recently celebrated its 80th anniversary, and Rabideau says student numbers are increasing. UNH has also expanded its occupational therapy pathways with the addition of the occupational therapy doctorate (OTD), which recently graduated its first class. Rabideau says consistently bringing professionals to UNH strengthens connections between the university and the state's occupational therapy community while also giving students a glimpse of where their education can take them. "It's a reminder of their next step for them, too," Rabideau says. "It's like, 'Oh, this is the next real thing for me,' which can be really fun." Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: What Makes a Walk in the Woods Good for Your Mental Health? UNH Research Offers New Clues - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH researchers studied visitors to College Woods to better understand how perceptions of biodiversity and natural sounds relate to mental well-being. Ever wonder why a walk through College Woods after spending hours studying can do wonders for your mood? While past research has shown that spending time outdoors can improve mental well-being, new UNH research offers a closer look at what makes those experiences so beneficial. In a yearlong study at College Woods, researchers found that visitors' perceptions of biodiversity — the many species living in the woods — and the sounds they experienced were closely linked to mental well-being. They also found that something as simple as an educational sign highlighting biodiversity could give visitors' moods an additional boost. The study, published in Landscape and Urban Planning, was led by an interdisciplinary team that included Lauren Ferguson, assistant professor of recreation management and policy, Remington Moll, associate professor of natural resources and the environment, Laura Kloepper, associate professor of biological sciences, UNH graduate student Anna Frisbie, and Karina Sanchez, assistant professor of biology from California State University, Dominguez Hills. “Previous nature-health research had a major limitation: it could tell us that ‘biodiversity is good for mental health’ but couldn't tell land managers, park planners, or healthcare providers what to actually do with that information,” Ferguson says. “The research lacked specificity about which aspects of biodiversity matter most and how to enhance the mental health benefits of nature visits.” Between June 2023 and May 2024, researchers surveyed visitors to College Woods, a 230-acre natural area bordering the UNH campus, collecting 641 matched surveys before and after their visits. They also measured biodiversity using wildlife cameras, bird surveys, and vegetation records. Visitors reported more positive emotions, fewer negative emotions, and greater feelings of restoration, including relaxation and recovery from mental fatigue, after spending time in the woods. On average, participants' self-reported restoration scores increased by nearly 30% following their visits. Additionally, researchers found that visitors' overall perceptions of biodiversity were stronger predictors of mental well-being than the actual number of bird and mammal species researchers measured. The pleasantness of the sounds visitors experienced, such as birdsong, rustling leaves, and flowing water, was another strong predictor. The study also found that season influenced visitors' experiences. Participants reported greater feelings of restoration during spring and summer, but improvements in mood were observed regardless of season. “I was somewhat surprised by these findings; however, I've had similar results in another project,” Ferguson says. “I think that visitors to parks are more comfortable perceiving overall biodiversity and forest health and perhaps less comfortable identifying and counting specific species. This is something that we will continue to examine in future research.” To explore whether helping visitors recognize biodiversity could influence their experiences, the researchers placed an educational sign near the College Woods trail entrance during designated periods and removed it during others. The sign, titled "Meet the neighbors!" highlighted the forest's wildlife, including more than 20 mammal species, 50 bird species, and 110 plant and tree species. It encouraged visitors to look and listen for different species. Visitors who encountered the sign perceived slightly greater biodiversity than those who didn't. The sign was also positively associated with positive mood, although it did not show a meaningful relationship with reductions in negative emotions or increased restoration. “We think the signs may help people become more aware of the biodiversity around them and notice species they might otherwise miss,” Ferguson says. “That can create a stronger, more mindful connection with nature and turn a casual walk in the woods into a more restorative experience.” By shedding light on what makes time in nature beneficial, the findings offer insights for park managers, urban planners, and others responsible for maintaining public green space. “Our research shows that educational signs about biodiversity were linked to a boost in positive mood during forest visits,” Ferguson says. “Biodiversity education signs are a simple, inexpensive tool that forest managers can use to enhance those benefits.” For a university campus, where students often face academic pressures and mental-health challenges, the findings also underscore the potential value of accessible natural spaces such as College Woods, Ferguson adds. “I hope that people start to view small community forests like College Woods and other parks as more than just a space for recreation, but as critical health infrastructure,” Ferguson says. While the findings are specific to College Woods, where most participants were repeat visitors and many were connected to the university, Ferguson sees opportunities to build on the research. Future studies could explore whether similar results hold in other natural settings, incorporate physiological measures of well-being, and examine how different types of educational signage influence visitors' experiences. title: UNH Students Speak Amid Lawsuit Challenging Restriction of Using Student IDs to Vote - InDepthNH.org

InDepthNH.org (https://indepthnh.org/2026/10/19/unh-students-speak-amid-lawsuit-challenging-restriction-of-using-student-ids-to-vote/) DURHAM — Some students at University of New Hampshire are speaking out in the wake of a lawsuit that challenges the use of student IDs to vote, expressing concerns that it would cause confusion among young voters and limit their ability to participate in politics. House Bill 323 — which made student IDs a no longer valid form of identification to obtain a ballot — was signed into law by Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte in April. That same month, Secretary of State David Scanlan released a directive advising that student IDs cannot be used as proof of ID when registering to vote, requesting an absentee ballot, or checking in to vote in an election. A lawsuit was filed in August by Free Speech for People, representing Coalition for Open Democracy (a voter education and outreach group) asking the Court to enjoin both HB 323 and Scanlan’s directive before the election. “I believe that student IDs are valid in the court system, and because a student ID is just enough of identification like a real ID would be. I don’t know why you need to bring extra identification… I feel like college students don’t really bring — or have other forms of identification, especially since they have a home, but they’re not there very often — so, they keep all of their identification at home. So, it takes a toll on how many people are able to vote,” UNH student Dalaney Trudeau said Monday. Secretary of State Scanlan’s motion for a stay on the legal proceedings for the lawsuit was denied by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, though an emergency stay has been requested from the U.S. Supreme Court. Previously, a federal judge ruled that student IDs can still be considered by election officials at polling places as evidence of voter identity. They can still be used for considering voter identification if supplemented with other documentation. Head of UNH’s Media Relations Tania DeLuzuriaga said the university has not taken a position on the lawsuit. Michael Garrity, spokesman for the New Hampshire Office of the Attorney General, said there were no updates to the case as of Monday. “The State has asked the United States Supreme Court for an emergency stay in this matter. New Hampshire has a strong interest in ensuring that its election laws are applied consistently and that local election officials have clear, workable guidance in administering elections,” Garrity said. Prime sponsor of HB 323, Rep. Donald McFarlane, R-Orange, did not respond for comment. Co-sponsor Rep. Ross Berry, R-Weare, insisted that the public supports the measure. When asked about the concerns from UNH students that the situation would cause confusion among young voters and how they feel it could limit the amounts of students who vote, Berry said: “I don’t see how that is a thing.” Another student, Olivia Rose of Barrington, said it’s unacceptable and restricting their ability to vote doesn’t seem appropriate. She said it would make students more detached from politics because they won’t feel the need to look into what’s going on politically (and) that limiting their ability to vote and participate in politics would make them less likely to try. UNH student Kai Shanahan said being able to use student IDs is a good way to prove voter identification “because sometimes, students aren’t able to get a driver’s license or a non-driver’s ID. Especially since for a lot of people at college, it’s their first time being out of the house.” Shanahan added she feels it would cause more confusion for young voters in college and “definitely stop people from voting.” According to data from July by the Civics Center — a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization aimed at encouraging young people to vote — noted that just 7% of 18-year-olds are registered to vote in the state as of March 31. It also highlighted how “there is not a single county in the state where the rate was at 10% or more as of March.” The data shows that, per county, the various rates of 18-year-olds registered to vote are: Student James Frady, from Massachusetts, said he wasn’t aware of the lawsuit but if a student ID is supplemented with other forms of documentation to prove voter identification that “I see it as a valid marker that you’re here at UNH and you’re in the system.” “I’m from Massachusetts, and I voted in Massachusetts, but I think it’s definitely a hassle to get all the documents in order. And that could definitely make it easier if student IDs were allowed as an option,” Frady said. House Democratic Leader Rep. Alexis Simpson, D-Exeter said: “Eligible voters have a fundamental right to cast a ballot, and deliberately removing ways to prove identity is voter suppression. For six years, Republicans have made it harder to register, vote absentee, and prove identity at the polls as the cost of living has skyrocketed. If Republicans had an agenda Granite Staters wanted, they would run on that instead of attacking the right to vote.” House Majority Leader Jason Osborne, R-Auburn said he did not have any comments on the matter. title: University of New Haven student killed by wrong-way driver remembered as campus leader - WFSB
content:
NEW HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - Ryan O’Shea, a University of New Haven student described as a club hockey captain, fraternity president and campus leader, was killed by a wrong-way driver in North Haven on Friday night. O’Shea, 21, was set to graduate in the spring. He had interned with the NYPD and wanted to become a police officer with the department after graduation. O’Shea was the assistant captain of UNH’s club hockey team. The team had a game Friday night, and O’Shea was driving back to campus afterward. He was on Route 91 South in North Haven just before midnight when state police say 31-year-old Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, of Bridgeport, was driving the wrong way and crashed into O’Shea head-on. O’Shea was then hit by two other drivers and died. Carmona-Lopez is in the hospital fighting for his life. He has not been charged, and state police are still investigating. Ophelie Rowe-Allen, vice president of student affairs at UNH, said O’Shea represented the university well. “Our students are always looking for opportunities on campus to be leaders, good citizens, good stewardesses and to represent the university at all times and that’s what Ryan was doing for us,” Rowe-Allen said. “That was very hard to hear and to know Ryan was coming from a hockey game with his teammates, was very excited and ready for the next game the following day,” Rowe-Allen said. “It’s a very, very sad time for us,” Rowe-Allen said. In a statement, O’Shea’s teammates wrote: “Ryan embodied what it meant to be a Charger. His infectious personality and sense of humor lit up our locker room.” Jackson Brentson, a UNH senior, said O’Shea had an impact on those around him. “I know people who knew him and it seems he had an impact on people and people cared about him and it’s just really awful that something like were to happen,” Brentson said. “I hope the family has a lot of support right now. It’s unimaginable, just awful,” Brentson said. School officials have been in touch with O’Shea’s family. His funeral is set for Friday. The university is setting up travel accommodations for students and offering counseling. O’Shea was from Stony Point, New York, about 40 miles north of Manhattan. O’Shea’s death is the second wrong-way crash death in Connecticut this year. There has been a significant drop in those deaths in recent years: 23 in 2022, 13 in 2024, and seven last year. The Connecticut Department of Transportation has installed 300 wrong-way detection systems on highway on-ramps around the state. The systems have gone off 1,300 times, and in 1,100 of those cases, drivers self-corrected before getting onto the highway. title: From the classroom to the coast: An environmental conservation major's journey at UNH - University of New Hampshire
content: Growing up in New Hampshire, this senior knew early on that a career path protecting the natural world was in her future. What was unknown was exactly where that path would lead. Senior Julia Briggaman, an environmental conservation and sustainability major with a minor in marine policy, reflects on UNH experiences like conducting seal ethograms on Appledore Island, identifying a humpback whale by name, discovering a passion for marine policy, and learning to embrace uncertainty along the way. Explore environmental conservation & sustainabilityty Why did you choose UNH? It felt like the perfect fit for who I am and what I value. Growing up in New Hampshire, I spent much of my childhood outdoors, hunting, fishing, kayaking, skiing, and exploring the coast. These experiences, along with being raised with a strong appreciation for conservation, sparked my passion for environmental science. UNH stood out because of its strong environmental and marine science programs, hands-on learning opportunities, and proximity to diverse ecosystems, making it the perfect place to pursue my education and prepare for a career in conservation. What's something about UNH that most people don't know? The incredible number of opportunities available beyond the classroom. From clubs and campus events to research, internships, volunteer experiences, and jobs, there are endless ways to get involved and grow. My time at UNH has helped shape who I am by allowing me to explore new interests, deepen my passion for ocean conservation, and gain experiences that have influenced myself as a person and my goals for the future. I’d tell her that it’s okay not to have everything figured out. College is about exploring, growing, and discovering what truly matters to you. Take every opportunity that comes your way, even if it feels intimidating. Apply for the internship, join the club, take the class, and say yes to new experiences. Some of the most meaningful moments of my college career came from stepping outside my comfort zone. Especially in the environmental field, there are so many paths to explore, so embrace the uncertainty and trust that each experience will help guide you toward the future that’s right for you. What's your favorite course you've taken at UNH? Taking Marine Mammal Biology at the Isles of Shoals was truly life-changing, with incredible professors, new friendships, and unforgettable hands-on learning. Living and learning on Appledore Island allowed me to fully immerse myself in marine science from the excitement of boating to Appledore, to conducting seal ethograms, and dodging gulls on the beautiful coastal shore. The excitement of being surrounded by people who shared my passion for the ocean created an incredible sense of community. This experience deepened my love for marine conservation and gave me a renewed sense of purpose and excitement for my future as a marine biologist. Why did you choose your major? I’m majoring in environmental conservation and sustainability (ECS) because I knew I wanted a career focused on protecting the environment, but I wanted the flexibility to explore my interests. As a freshman, I was torn between zoology and marine biology, so ECS gave me a strong foundation while allowing me to discover my path. Through a semester-long environmental policy project on North Atlantic right whales, I found my passion for marine conservation and policy, which lead me to pursue a minor in marine policy. I love that ECS allows students to explore different areas, gain hands-on experience, and find the field that truly inspires them. Where have you found a sense of community at UNH? One of the biggest places I’ve found a sense of community through UNH is outside of campus. I love meeting people who also go to UNH and instantly finding connections through shared classes, experiences, friends, or places we’ve been. Whether through a summer job, internship, or everyday life, these connections make UNH feel like a family that extends far beyond Durham. No matter where you go, you’re likely to find another Wildcat. Reflecting on your time at UNH, what's an experience that stands out to you? Marine Mammal Biology at the Isles of Shoals stands out the most. The moment I saw my first Humpback whale breach is something I will never forget. After doing fluke identification the day before, we were able to identify the whale as “Sedge” in that moment. Watching a whale that I could recognize by name brought everything I had worked for at UNH to life. It deepened my love for the ocean, strengthened my passion for marine conservation, and further excited me for the field I chose to pursue. What's your favorite spot in Durham? The big reading room in Dimond Library. I’ve spent countless hours there, and it has become one of the places I associate most with my time at UNH. Whether it’s a crisp fall afternoon or snowy winter day, grabbing a coffee from Zeke’s and settling by the windows to study or enjoy the quiet atmosphere is one of my favorite campus traditions. What are your aspirations for the future? My goal for the future is to build a career studying and protecting marine mammals through research and conservation. I hope to move south after graduation to continue working in marine environments. UNH is helping me reach these goals through a strong foundation in environmental science, hands-on field experiences, and opportunities like Shoals Marine Laboratory and my work at the Seacoast Science Center. Tell us about a part of your college experience that wasn't what you thought it was going to be. I came to UNH thinking I needed to have my entire future planned out, but I learned that college is about exploring, growing, and discovering what truly inspires you. Through experiences like finding my passion for marine biology, discovering yoga, embracing traveling, and learning to take more opportunities, I gained confidence and learned to embrace uncertainty. UNH has not only prepared me for my career but has helped shape who I am today. Have you received any scholarships and what have you been able to do or accomplish at UNH because of them? I am incredibly grateful for the scholarships I have received from UNH and outside organizations. Their generosity has allowed me to continue my education, pursue opportunities that shaped my future, and focus on building a career in environmental conservation. They have made a life-changing impact by making my dreams more achievable and reducing the financial barriers of my college journey. I hope to honor their support by using my education to make a meaningful difference in protecting our marine ecosystems. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: What Do History Majors Do? - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you fascinated with how things used to be and what that means for us now? History is the study of the past and how that knowledge can inform the present and the future. Meet William Kirkpatrick '26, a history major from Eliot, Maine, who has found a close community on the UNH campus, with plenty of room to explore by studying how dinosaur bones may have influenced Greek mythology and by studying abroad in Turkey. William Kirkpatrick: I chose UNH because the campus has the appeal of the beautiful small schools of New England while providing enough opportunities, classes, and people to feel like a significant step up from my small Maine high school. Growing up with two parents who worked at UNH, I also had the opportunity to meet some of the professors, faculty, and staff, all of whom were extremely kind and welcoming. It seemed like an easy choice. My favorite thing about COLA is that almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before. Coming in my first year, I certainly didn't think I would write a final paper two years later comparing Odysseus in Homer's "The Odyssey" to Mad Max. I can't think of another college that would actively encourage such ambitions. "Almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before." I love the history department because of the many subjects it offers. One class will have me writing about medieval hunting practices, and the next will provide the opportunity to present about why dinosaur bones have heavily influenced Greek mythology. I believe, above all, that my liberal arts education has given me the ability to think critically and present my thoughts in a convincing manner after considering the presented material. Paraphrasing Professor Gregory McMahon, a liberal arts education is a lesson in persuasion, critical thinking, and independence presented in the most fascinating way possible. I agree! My most impactful professors are both Professor Gregory McMahon and Professor David Bachrach. During my first semester freshman year, Professor Bachrach taught me how to write like a historian and encouraged me to reach out to him with drafts of all my papers. I still refer to some of my papers from that year for format and grammar. Then, in my sophomore year, Professor McMahon helped me understand how fun it is to create new ideas based on ancient sources and supported me when I would come to him with frankly crazy ideas for papers. Professor McMahon sent me to study abroad on his archaeological dig in Turkey this summer. I never took people who said that studying abroad would change your life seriously, because how could it? However, my time in Turkey is one of the highlights of my college experience and probably my life. It's such a vastly different culture from ours, but I fit right in since everyone I met treated me as if they had known me their whole life. In addition to the amazing Turkish culture, getting to see, touch, and excavate the artifacts that I've spent so much of my college career reading about, analyzing, and writing about is a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I can hopefully turn into a twice-in-a-lifetime experience in the near future. This scholarship allowed me to free up money to study abroad in Turkey this summer. I will be forever grateful that UNH allowed me the opportunity to experience Turkish culture from a perspective that many people are not afforded. There are two pieces of advice I would give my freshman self. The first is to explore the campus earlier. There are many cool areas, such as College Woods, the Fishbowl, and the tennis courts, that I never really used until later on. UNH is meant to be explored, and everyone has their favorite spot on campus to study and hang out. The second piece is to study abroad earlier. If I had the chance to go on a second trip before graduation, I would have taken it immediately. I was originally scared that I would feel alone, homesick, and out of place, but I found the opposite was true. There will never be another opportunity to experience international culture like that offered in college, so why not take it? I have found a sense of community within my friend group. Most of us met during the "Become the Roar" tradition during orientation, and we have stayed very close friends throughout all four years. My freshman year roommate is still my best friend, and all of us shared an eight-person suite in Mills Hall during my sophomore year. One thing people might be surprised to learn about me is that during the summers, I work as a groundskeeper for my local cemetery. After someone learns this, I am immediately asked if I bury the people, too, which, yes, I do. However, I am hopefully far from the cemetery groundskeeper stereotype.
